SearchHow we decideRulings

Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Time, the calendar & feasts

modern adjective

of the present or recent times

also modern times, the moderns, up to date

classical

Cic. N.D. 2.6: recentiōre memoriā (Lewis & Short)
Tac. Ann. 3.18: recentium seu veterum
M-O s.v. modern: recentior

recēns, recentis

recent, modern

recentiōre memoriā, in more recent times.

Examples

  • mihi quantō plūra recentium seu veterum revolvō, tantō magis lūdibria rērum mortālium cūnctīs in negōtiīs obversantur

    the more I turn over the events of modern times and of old, the more the mockery of human affairs meets me in everythingTac. Ann. 3.18

  • disces tū quidem ā prīncipe hujus aetātis philosophōrum

    you will learn, of course, from the foremost philosopher of our timeCic. Off. 1.2

Other words

  • hujus aetātis — of this age, of our time

    also used · classical · Cic. Off. 1.2: ā prīncipe hujus aetātis philosophōrum

  • hodiernus, hodierna, hodiernum — of today; present-day

    also used · classical · Cic. Phil. 4.7: ex hodiernō ejus ēdictō (Lewis & Short); M-O s.v. modern, contemporary, of this age, current

    Of the present time in general only after Augustus (Lewis & Short); see current.

  • modernus, moderna, modernum — modern

    also used · late Latin · Cassiod. Var. 4.51 (Lewis & Short)

    Late Latin, from modo, just now, as hodiernus from hodiē; classical writers say recēns or hujus aetātis.

See also recent, current, new, today.

SourcesLewis & Short: recens · Lewis & Short: aetas · Lewis & Short: hodiernus · Lewis & Short: modernus

Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. modern; modern, contemporary, of this age, current.
